passages.title: Citizen Science and Biodiversity
passages.intro: An academic-style overview of biology, examining evidence and practical implications.
paras: Volunteer observers can collect data across areas too large for a small research team. Basic training can make observations more consistent between participants.
Records of rare species should be checked before being accepted. Weather conditions can affect whether an animal or plant is observed.
Online platforms allow records from many contributors to be combined. Taking part can increase participants' interest in scientific questions.
If volunteers concentrate in certain places, other areas may have fewer records. Researchers still need to interpret data and account for its limitations.

passages.title: Why Some Materials Self-Heal
passages.intro: An academic-style overview of engineering, examining evidence and practical implications.
paras: Some self-healing materials contain tiny capsules that release a repair agent when damaged. The extent to which a crack closes varies with the material and conditions.
Certain systems need an external trigger such as heat or light. A limited quantity of healing agent may be used up after repeated damage.
Laboratory tests are most useful when they reflect conditions materials will face. A repaired area may not regain all of its original mechanical strength.
Cost still limits the use of some self-healing technologies. Researchers are investigating uses in roads, bridges and other infrastructure.

passages.title: Urban Heat Islands
passages.intro: An academic-style overview of environment, examining evidence and practical implications.
paras: Concrete and asphalt absorb and store energy from sunlight. Where vegetation is scarce, less water evaporates from leaves and soil to cool the air.
Urban areas may stay warmer at night because built surfaces release stored heat. The cooling effect of trees depends on canopy size and where they are planted.
Some reflective surfaces absorb less solar energy than darker alternatives. Cities must balance cooling measures with other demands for urban space.
Older people and some people with health conditions can be more affected by extreme heat. Measurements at multiple sites show that heat varies from street to street.
